question.text: A Portfolio Manager that contravenes the SEBI Act, rules or regulations is liable to:

answer.text: Action under Chapter V of the SEBI Intermediaries Regulations, including suspension or cancellation of registration
A one-time warning only, with no further consequences
Mandatory revocation of the PAN of the Principal Officer
Criminal prosecution under the Companies Act in every case

explanation.text: The Logic: For default by a Portfolio Manager, the SEBI Intermediaries Regulations (Chapter V) provide the regulatory action toolkit — suspension of registration, cancellation of registration, prohibition from taking up new assignments or clients, debarment from accessing the securities market, and warning. The specific action is calibrated to the severity of the contravention, but the source of authority is Chapter V of the Intermediaries Regulations read together with the SEBI Act. The Trap: "A one-time warning only" understates SEBI's powers; warnings are one possible outcome but not the only one. "Mandatory PAN revocation" confuses securities-market sanctions with income-tax administration — SEBI does not revoke PANs. "Criminal prosecution under the Companies Act in every case" is wrong on two counts: prosecution depends on the facts, and the Companies Act is not the principal source of action against an erring SEBI-registered intermediary. Note: This framing is drawn from the NISM-Series-XXI-B workbook treatment of regulatory actions for default (e.g., page 152 in the cited edition), which references suspension, cancellation, prohibition of new assignments, debarment and warning. The original "Unlimited – cannot be waived" framing about negligence/misconduct liability is not stated on the cited pages (150, 152); page 150 says a discretionary PM agreement caps client liability at the client's invested amount.
